terms.grammar: obstō, obstāre, obstitī with the dative
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 112: cūr mihi tē offers ac meīs commodīs officis et obstās? (Lewis & Short)
Plaut. Curc. 284: nec quisquamst tam opulentus, quī mī obsistat in viā
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to stand against or in the way of a person or thing”, the classical sense of the word. Plautus’s running slave uses obsistere in viā of anyone who blocks the street. What one says next is concēde, “move over”.

terms.gloss: you’re in my light; you’re blocking me
terms.grammar: officiō, officere, offēcī, offectum with the dative
terms.comment: Of standing between someone and the sun, as Alexander stood before Diogenes.

phrases.latin: Obstās hominibus; concēde hūc ad mē.
phrases.english: You’re in people’s way; come over here to me.

phrases.latin: Concēde istūc paululum: audīn'? etiam nunc paululum: sat est.
phrases.english: Move over there a little — do you hear? — a little more — that’s enough.

phrases.latin: Nunc quidem paululum, inquit, ā sōle.
phrases.english: “Just now,” he said, “move a little out of my sun.”

sources: Lewis & Short: obsto · Lewis & Short: officio · Lewis & Short: concedo
